title: Same Shape Trap
question: A chef argues that because a cook must taste food while preparing it, a surgeon should operate on their own body during surgery. What is the central flaw?
choices: A shared surface word masks a relevant difference
The conclusion rests on a tested mechanism
The analogy is strong because both are skilled trades
The reasoning is circular but still convincing
correctAnswer: A shared surface word masks a relevant difference
correctExplanation: Right. Tasting is sampling for quality, not operating on yourself — the shared word hides wildly different actions.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: a shared surface word masks a relevant difference. The two roles share a vocabulary, not a method, and the whole conclusion rides on that coincidence.
lessonContent:
Surface wording can disguise a deep difference in action.
Analogy transfers only when the underlying mechanism matches.
Test whether the shared term means the same thing twice.
Name the relevant feature the comparison ignores.
Share this: find tonight one comparison that survives only on a shared word.

title: Old Law New Phone
question: A legislator says a rule for organising a bookshelf is so obviously sensible that the same plan must work for a national economy. Why does the comparison fail?
choices: The systems differ in complexity and feedback
The two cases follow exactly equal rules
Economies are merely larger bookshelves
The argument was never meant as a comparison
correctAnswer: The systems differ in complexity and feedback
correctExplanation: Right. A shelf is static and small; an economy is adaptive, with countless actors reacting to every rule.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the systems differ in complexity and feedback. Scale and feedback turn a tidy principle into a warning, because people respond to the plan in ways shelves never do.
lessonContent:
Scale can change what a rule actually does.
Systems with feedback behave unlike static ones.
Check whether both cases respond to intervention.
Complexity is a relevant difference, not a detail.
Share this: name tonight one plan that needs a different version at a larger scale.

title: Both Sides Wrong
question: Someone breaks a promise and someone else cheats on a test. Because both acted wrongly, an arguer concludes the two offences are equally serious. What is the mistake?
choices: Equal labels do not make equal magnitude
Broken promises are always the graver act
Cheating is never a matter of wrongdoing
Only one of the two sides was at fault
correctAnswer: Equal labels do not make equal magnitude
correctExplanation: Right. Calling both acts wrong says nothing about how wrong each one is — severity is a separate question.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: equal labels do not make equal magnitude. Sharing a category is not sharing a weight, and treating the two as identical erases the very trade-offs morality needs.
lessonContent:
Sharing a category is not sharing a degree.
Separate whether an act is wrong from how wrong it is.
Magnitude needs its own evidence and scale.
Watch for labels that flatten important differences.
Share this: weigh tonight two wrongs you know without using the same word for both.

title: One Shared Feature
question: Two plans both use the colour blue, and a manager concludes that whichever plan works better here will also work better abroad. What is the reasoning error?
choices: One shared feature is doing all the work
The plans are identical in every respect
Colour has no bearing on anything at all
Foreign markets should not be compared
correctAnswer: One shared feature is doing all the work
correctExplanation: Right. Blue is irrelevant to performance, so the resemblance proves nothing about how either plan behaves.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: one shared feature is doing all the work. An analogy needs relevant overlap, and an irrelevant trait cannot carry a conclusion about outcomes.
lessonContent:
Analogies need overlap that bears on the conclusion.
Irrelevant similarities are noise, not evidence.
Ask which shared feature could actually cause the result.
Distinguish decorative likeness from causal likeness.
Share this: spot tonight one argument that leans on a purely decorative similarity.

title: Irrelevant Disanalogy
question: An enthusiast says a bicycle and a corporation are alike because both have spokespeople, so a bike manual should guide a boardroom. Which reply best diagnoses the analogy?
choices: The comparison ignores the relevant domain difference
Corporations and bicycles share no traits at all
Repair manuals are useful in every setting
The analogy is sound but the conclusion is rude
correctAnswer: The comparison ignores the relevant domain difference
correctExplanation: Right. The shared word 'spokes' is a pun, and the domains of machines and governance behave nothing alike.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the comparison ignores the relevant domain difference. It is not that nothing is shared, but that what is shared cannot support the transfer of one domain's methods to the other.
lessonContent:
Some similarities are real yet useless for transfer.
A pun is not a structural resemblance.
Test whether the shared trait could bear the conclusion's weight.
Name the domain difference the analogy skips.
Share this: separate tonight a genuine similarity from a merely verbal one.

title: Precedent Transfer
question: A lawyer argues that a ruling about noisy neighbours settles a case about industrial pollution because both involve disturbance. When does the precedent actually transfer?
choices: Precedent transfers only when the mechanism transfers
Precedent always transfers whenever judges feel it fits
Noisy neighbours and polluters are legally identical
Precedent never transfers between distinct settings
correctAnswer: Precedent transfers only when the mechanism transfers
correctExplanation: Right. A ruling follows the legal reasoning that produced it, so the new case must share the mechanism, not just the mood.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: precedent transfers only when the mechanism transfers. Noise and toxic discharge may both annoy, but the duties, harms, and standards they trigger are entirely different.
lessonContent:
Rules travel with reasons, not with vibes.
A shared effect does not guarantee a shared mechanism.
Identify the principle a ruling actually rests on.
Match that principle to the new facts before transferring.
Share this: apply tonight one rule by first stating the reason behind it.

title: Same Outcome Same Cause
question: Two students both fail an exam. One never studied; the other was ill. A teacher blames laziness in both cases. What is the flaw?
choices: Similarity of outcome does not prove similarity of cause
Illness always explains every academic failure
Both students cannot possibly have failed fairly
Laziness is never a real explanation for anyone
correctAnswer: Similarity of outcome does not prove similarity of cause
correctExplanation: Right. One result can have many routes, so matching failures says nothing about matching reasons.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: similarity of outcome does not prove similarity of cause. Diagnosis requires looking at each path, not inferring the cause from the shared finish line.
lessonContent:
Results can converge from unrelated causes.
Never infer one cause from one shared outcome.
Investigate each case before generalising.
Treat correlation and causation as distinct tools.
Share this: ask tonight about two similar failures before assuming one reason.

title: Vivid Not Evidence
question: To prove a diet works, a speaker shows a dramatic before-and-after photo and asks the audience to be convinced. What is wrong with this argument?
choices: The vivid comparison substitutes for evidence
Photographs are always honest and reliable
Dieting has no measurable effects on anyone
The audience failed to appreciate the image
correctAnswer: The vivid comparison substitutes for evidence
correctExplanation: Right. A striking image is memorable, but a single anecdote cannot stand in for controlled results.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the vivid comparison substitutes for evidence. Vividness is a feature of presentation, not of proof, and it can make weak claims feel overwhelming.
lessonContent:
Vividness persuades without proving.
Memorable examples still need systematic support.
Separate presentation strength from evidential strength.
Ask what data would confirm the claim beyond one case.
Share this: notice tonight where a striking image is doing an argument's work.

title: Asymmetric Wrongs
question: An arguer says you cannot criticise a small theft by a citizen because a bank also broke the law. What is the defect in this comparison?
choices: Both sides are not symmetric because both erred somewhere
Banks are inherently more honest than citizens
Small thefts are the most serious of all crimes
Citizens are never permitted to commit crimes
correctAnswer: Both sides are not symmetric because both erred somewhere
correctExplanation: Right. Two wrongs of different size and character do not cancel out; the reply changes the subject instead of answering.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: both sides are not symmetric because both erred somewhere. The offender's own fault does not erase the citizen's, and treating them as equal is the real distortion.
lessonContent:
A counter-wrong does not nullify a first wrong.
Symmetry must be argued, not assumed from shared guilt.
Notice when a reply dodges rather than answers.
Compare like with like in scale and kind.
Share this: watch tonight for a defence that only changes the subject.

title: Map Is Not Territory
question: A strategist treats a simplified diagram of a city as if every feature of the real streets were captured in it. What mistake is being made?
choices: The map is not the territory it describes
Diagrams are useless for any real planning
Cities never change once they are mapped
The strategist should ignore the real streets
correctAnswer: The map is not the territory it describes
correctExplanation: Right. Every model omits something, and mistaking the abridgement for the place itself is what leads plans astray.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the map is not the territory it describes. The diagram is useful precisely because it leaves things out, but usefulness is not completeness.
lessonContent:
All models simplify by necessity.
Forgetting the omissions turns a tool into a trap.
Match the model's purpose to your question.
Return to the terrain before betting on the plan.
Share this: name tonight one thing a favourite model of yours leaves out.

title: Metaphor as Mechanism
question: Someone explains memory by saying the brain is a filing cabinet, then concludes memories must be stored in alphabetical order. What error has occurred?
choices: A metaphor is being treated as a mechanism
Filing cabinets are poorly understood devices
Memory research has produced no useful results
The brain contains no physical structures at all
correctAnswer: A metaphor is being treated as a mechanism
correctExplanation: Right. The cabinet is a helpful image, but an image has no gears, so its incidental features carry no real predictions.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: a metaphor is being treated as a mechanism. Pictures aid intuition, yet only an actual mechanism can license claims about how something must work.
lessonContent:
Metaphors illuminate without explaining.
Do not infer details from a figure of speech.
Ask what independent process could produce the result.
Keep illustration separate from mechanism.
Share this: catch tonight one metaphor you have started taking literally.

title: Question-Begging Analogy
question: A speaker claims that since a good team is a family, members owe absolute obedience, because families demand absolute obedience. What is the flaw?
choices: The analogy begs the question it was meant to answer
Teams and families have nothing in common at all
Obedience is always required inside every group
The speaker has proven the conclusion properly
correctAnswer: The analogy begs the question it was meant to answer
correctExplanation: Right. The claim to be supported is smuggled into the comparison, so the argument assumes what it set out to show.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the analogy begs the question it was meant to answer. The disputed feature is loaded into the premise, which turns the reasoning into a circle.
lessonContent:
Check whether the premise already contains the conclusion.
Analogiests can smuggle in the very point at issue.
A valid argument cannot assume its own result.
Restate the claim without the analogy to test it.
Share this: strip tonight an argument of its metaphor and see what remains.

title: Scale Changes Properties
question: Because a paper boat floats, a child concludes that a steel ship of the same shape must also float. The reasoning needs which correction?
choices: Scale changes the properties being compared
Steel vessels are simply paper in disguise
Nothing large can ever be made to float
The child's conclusion was fully justified
correctAnswer: Scale changes the properties being compared
correctExplanation: Right. The child's conclusion happens to be true, but not for the reason given — material and buoyancy behave differently at scale.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: scale changes the properties being compared. Weight grows with volume while the hull's support grows differently, so an inference from a small model needs more than shape.
lessonContent:
Properties can shift as size increases.
Shape alone rarely determines behaviour at scale.
Small models test feasibility, not certainty.
Recheck assumptions whenever magnitude changes.
Share this: notice tonight one thing that behaves differently when made much bigger.

title: Fallacy of One Case
question: One rainy Monday had low sales, so a manager declares that rain always depresses sales everywhere. Which diagnosis fits best?
choices: The analogy commits the fallacy of the single case
Rain reliably lowers sales in every market
One Monday cannot be measured at all
Sales data should never be collected
correctAnswer: The analogy commits the fallacy of the single case
correctExplanation: Right. A single observation cannot support a universal rule, no matter how tidy it looks.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the analogy commits the fallacy of the single case. One rainy Monday might be a coincidence or a local quirk, so generality needs many cases and a comparison group.
lessonContent:
A single instance cannot ground a universal rule.
Generality needs many cases and a contrast.
Watch for confident claims built from one observation.
Ask for the base rate before accepting a trend.
Share this: question tonight one sweeping claim that rests on a lone example.

title: One Example Rule
question: A traveller meets one rude waiter in a city and concludes that everyone there is rude. What is the reasoning error?
choices: One example is stretched into a general rule
Waiters are the best judges of a whole city
Cities can have only one waiter each
The traveller's experience was impossible
correctAnswer: One example is stretched into a general rule
correctExplanation: Right. A sample of one says almost nothing about a population, however striking the encounter felt.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: one example is stretched into a general rule. The traveller generalises from an unrepresentative moment, and strong feelings make small samples feel conclusive.
lessonContent:
Samples must be large enough to support a claim.
Emotion can disguise a tiny sample as proof.
Ask how representative the example really is.
Withhold general verdicts until the evidence widens.
Share this: catch tonight one broad conclusion drawn from a single person.

title: Whatabout Conduct
question: Asked about a company's emissions, a spokesperson replies that another firm littered last year, so the question should be dropped. What is this manoeuvre?
choices: Whataboutism compares conduct rather than the argument
The spokesperson answered the question directly
Littering is worse than every other offence
Companies should never be asked about emissions
correctAnswer: Whataboutism compares conduct rather than the argument
correctExplanation: Right. The reply shifts attention to a different party instead of addressing the question that was asked.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: whataboutism compares conduct rather than the argument. Even a genuine fault elsewhere is irrelevant to whether this company's emissions are a problem.
lessonContent:
Changing the subject is not answering.
Another's conduct cannot settle this question.
Notice when a reply redirects rather than replies.
Return the discussion to the original claim.
Share this: hold tonight one conversation to its original question.

title: Smuggled Value
question: An article calls one method clean and another dirty before presenting any data, then argues the first is superior. What is the problem?
choices: The comparison smuggles in a value judgment
Data are irrelevant to every comparison
Cleanliness is a measurable physical property
The second method is definitely the better one
correctAnswer: The comparison smuggles in a value judgment
correctExplanation: Right. Loading the labels with approval does the arguing before a single fact arrives.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the comparison smuggles in a value judgment. Word choice prejudges the question, so the reader is persuaded by framing rather than by evidence.
lessonContent:
Labels can carry hidden verdicts.
Choose neutral terms before weighing evidence.
Notice framing that steers conclusions in advance.
Separate description from evaluation.
Share this: rewrite tonight one loaded description in neutral words.

title: Natural Is Good
question: A label claims a product is superior because its ingredients are natural rather than synthetic. What is the inferential gap?
choices: Natural is not a synonym for good
Synthetic substances are always harmless
Labels are legally required to be true
Nature contains nothing dangerous at all
correctAnswer: Natural is not a synonym for good
correctExplanation: Right. Origin says nothing about safety or quality — many natural things are deadly and many synthetic ones are beneficial.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: natural is not a synonym for good. The argument slides from a descriptive fact about origin to a value judgment about worth, which needs its own support.
lessonContent:
Origin and value are separate questions.
Natural does not imply safe, and synthetic does not imply harmful.
Demand evidence for the leap from source to quality.
Watch for pleasant words doing logical work.
Share this: examine tonight one 'natural' claim and ask what it actually guarantees.

title: Trying Same Way
question: When a study method failed for one student, a coach says the student simply must try harder and repeat exactly the same routine. What is the flaw?
choices: Trying harder is not the same as trying the same way
Effort is completely irrelevant to all learning
Study methods can never be improved by anyone
The student's failure proves the method works
correctAnswer: Trying harder is not the same as trying the same way
correctExplanation: Right. More effort on a faulty method often deepens the rut, since intensity cannot repair an inappropriate approach.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: trying harder is not the same as trying the same way. Persistence matters, but repeating an unsuitable routine just spends more energy on the same mistake.
lessonContent:
Effort and method are different variables.
More intensity on a bad method wastes resources.
Diagnose the approach before demanding more grit.
Change one variable at a time when progress stalls.
Share this: review tonight one struggle where the method, not the effort, needs changing.

title: Middle Not True
question: Two experts disagree about a medical dose, so a journalist concludes the correct amount is exactly halfway between their numbers. What is the error?
choices: The middle option is not automatically the true one
Experts never disagree about medical doses
Halfway values are always the safest choice
Journalists should not report on medicine
correctAnswer: The middle option is not automatically the true one
correctExplanation: Right. Splitting a difference feels fair but has no evidential basis — one expert may simply be mistaken.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the middle option is not automatically the true one. Truth is not a compromise between positions, and averaging them can land on a dose neither side supports.
lessonContent:
Fairness is not the same as accuracy.
A midpoint between claims is not thereby true.
Weigh the evidence behind each position separately.
Do not let conflict resolution settle empirical questions.
Share this: resist tonight the urge to split a disagreement down the middle.

title: Anecdote Not Mechanism
question: A supplement seller cites one customer who felt better after taking it as proof that the product works for everyone. What is missing?
choices: An anecdote is not a mechanism
Customers are never reliable witnesses
Supplements always work for every person
Feeling better proves a product is effective
correctAnswer: An anecdote is not a mechanism
correctExplanation: Right. Feeling better may come from time, expectation, or coincidence, and none of those paths are the product working.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: an anecdote is not a mechanism. A single recovery story cannot show why the outcome occurred or whether the product caused it at all.
lessonContent:
Personal stories cannot isolate a cause.
Recovery has many possible explanations besides a product.
Mechanisms require controlled comparison.
Ask what would have happened without the intervention.
Share this: question tonight one testimonial about what actually caused the improvement.

title: Irrelevant Domain
question: A debater argues that because chess rewards patience, the same patience must win every negotiation. Why is the analogy weak?
choices: The analogy's domain is irrelevant to the claim
Chess and negotiation are the same activity
Patience never helps in any board game
Negotiations require no skill whatsoever
correctAnswer: The analogy's domain is irrelevant to the claim
correctExplanation: Right. Patience may help in both, but the claim covers all negotiations, and the chess setting cannot support that scope.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the analogy's domain is irrelevant to the claim. Similar virtues can appear in different activities without one guaranteeing success in the other.
lessonContent:
A virtue's value is relative to its setting.
Different activities reward the same trait differently.
Check whether the borrowed domain covers the conclusion.
Test the claim inside the target setting.
Share this: list tonight one skill that helps in one arena but not another.

title: Proves Too Much
question: A defence of astrology notes that its predictions feel accurate, which would equally justify any fortune-telling system. What is the flaw?
choices: The analogy proves too much to be useful
Fortune-telling systems are all scientifically sound
Feeling accurate is the best test of truth
Astrology has no competitors of any kind
correctAnswer: The analogy proves too much to be useful
correctExplanation: Right. A test that passes every system cannot distinguish the good from the worthless, so it supports nothing in particular.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the analogy proves too much to be useful. When the same reasoning would validate any rival, it has no discriminating power and cannot establish the claim.
lessonContent:
A test must be able to fail something.
Evidence that fits every outcome distinguishes nothing.
Ask whether a rival could use the same reasoning.
Prefer criteria with discriminating power.
Share this: check tonight whether one of your standards could ever rule anything out.

title: The Word Just
question: An arguer says a hospital is just a business, therefore it should cut every unprofitable ward. What does the word just conceal?
choices: The word just hides an unsupported equivalence
Hospitals genuinely are ordinary shops
Profit is the only measure of any value
Wards are never expensive to operate
correctAnswer: The word just hides an unsupported equivalence
correctExplanation: Right. 'Just' asserts that hospitals are nothing more than businesses, which is the very claim that needed proving.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the word just hides an unsupported equivalence. The little word flattens a contested comparison into a premise, smuggling the conclusion into the setup.
lessonContent:
Small words can smuggle large claims.
'Just' and 'merely' often assert an unproven reduction.
Notice when equivalence is assumed rather than argued.
Remove the qualifier and test the claim plainly.
Share this: spot tonight one 'just' that quietly assumes the point at issue.

title: Kinds Apart
question: A reviewer says a hammer is like a lawyer because both handle problems, then argues a hammer should be allowed to advise clients. What is the fundamental error?
choices: The two items belong to different logical categories
Hammers and lawyers are essentially interchangeable
Legal advice is a form of manual labour
The reviewer correctly matched two professions
correctAnswer: The two items belong to different logical categories
correctExplanation: Right. A tool and a professional are different kinds of thing, so capacities belonging to one cannot be reassigned to the other.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the two items belong to different logical categories. Comparing across kinds can suggest shared abilities that the categories themselves rule out.
lessonContent:
Comparisons must respect what kind of thing each item is.
Capacities do not transfer across category boundaries.
Ask whether the two belong to the same logical type.
Beware analogies that blur object with agent.
Share this: name tonight one comparison that quietly crosses between kinds.
